processes.title: Sell from Stock
processes.memory_hook: Own stock, own delivery, normal O2C.
processes.business_intent: Use the standard fulfillment path when the selling company owns the stock and delivers it through its normal shipping execution.

control_plane.control: sales document type and item category
control_plane.why: define order/item behavior and follow-on relevance
controls requirements, ATP and delivery relevance
drive fulfillment location and dates
drive commercial value and invoice creation

data_hinges.changes: availability context, shipping point, route and fulfillment dates
shipping geography, partner data and downstream logistics context
scheduling and availability result

impact_summary: Inventory leaves own stock at PGI; billing follows the delivery; the process is the reference pattern used to compare special variants.
constraints: A standard-looking order can still branch through aATP, TM, GTS, product compliance, credit, output, or custom logic.
Scope-item availability and exact apps differ by deployment and release.
lead_questions: What makes this item non-standard?
Which determination changes if plant or ship-to changes?
Which external capability owns a decision that looks like SD?

processes.title: Sales Quotation
processes.business_intent: Create a time-bounded commercial offer that can later become a sales order while preserving reference and commercial context.

control_plane.why: sets document behavior and follow-on rules
defines when the offer can be used
decides what moves into the sales order
can prevent subsequent order creation

data_hinges.changes: whether a subsequent order can still be created
expected value / prioritization, not the legal commitment
how much remains available for subsequent orders

impact_summary: No goods movement by itself; the important impact is commercial commitment and what is inherited by the follow-on order.
constraints: Fully referenced, fully rejected, incomplete, or approval-blocked quotations can prevent subsequent order creation.
Availability/allocation behavior depends on activated capabilities.
lead_questions: What must be frozen in the quotation versus redetermined in the order?
Does the customer expect the quoted date to be reserved or merely estimated?
Which copy-control rule owns the disputed value?

processes.title: Free-of-Charge Delivery
processes.memory_hook: Move goods without charging the customer.
processes.business_intent: Send samples, replacements, or other non-charged goods while keeping logistics execution explicit.

control_plane.why: separates the flow from normal commercial sales
records why value is being given away
prevents normal customer billing

data_hinges.changes: completeness and business justification
stock, delivery and shipping execution
delivery and billing behavior

impact_summary: Stock and cost can move even when customer revenue does not; this is why free-of-charge is not 'just price = zero'.
constraints: Billing behavior must stay distinct from a discounted normal sale.
Authorization and audit expectations usually matter because value leaves inventory without revenue.
lead_questions: Why is this free?
Who approves the economic give-away?
Should the downstream accounting or profitability treatment differ from normal sales?

processes.title: Long-Term Contract Family and Release Scope
processes.memory_hook: We first decide what the customer commits to; only then do we decide how execution is released.
processes.business_intent: We use this family to design long-term customer commitments without mixing quantity contracts, value contracts, master contracts, service contracts, scheduling agreements, and product-eligibility controls into one document pattern.

modes.title: Quantity contract
modes.memory: We agree a target quantity for defined products. We consume the remaining quantity through release orders when the customer is ready to call off goods.

modes.title: Value contract
modes.memory: We agree a target value. We consume that value through release orders and can restrict the releasable product scope according to the contract design.

modes.title: Master contract
modes.memory: We use an umbrella document to group lower-level contracts and keep common terms consistent. We do not treat it as the normal release-order demand object.

modes.title: Service contract boundary
modes.memory: We treat long-term service coverage as a neighboring Service model, not as the ordinary goods release-order chain.

control_plane.why: separates quantity, value, umbrella, and service semantics before execution rules are designed
defines when release orders or contract coverage may apply
creates the goods-contract document link and decides which data is copied or redetermined
we can bill the contract directly on planned dates and partial values; changes to target value adjust still-open billing dates
we can request a down payment from the contract and keep release-order schedule lines blocked until the required payment is received
we use the Outline Agrmt Mess. setting in the target order type when we want SAP to search for open outline agreements during order creation

current cloud model: create the hierarchy, assign products to nodes, assign the hierarchy for Sales to sales organization/distribution channel with validity, then use a hierarchy node in the value contract; release products must belong to that node

classic model: maintain the material list and validity in an assortment module, reference the module from the value contract, and release only valid materials for the contract sales area; verify availability in the target S/4HANA deployment
different problem: configure condition tables, access sequences, listing/exclusion types and procedures, then maintain condition records to control what a customer may buy in sales documents
different industry model: products are assigned to assortment modules/assortments and assortments to sites; listing conditions and periods control what a site can procure or sell
controls which partner may call off goods against the contract
controls what happens when released quantity or value approaches or exceeds the remaining target
controls which common data is inherited by lower-level contracts in the classic master-contract model

control_plane.control: service contract determination and billing plan
control_plane.why: belongs to the Service contract model and should not be designed as if it were a normal SD goods release
we decide whether a releasing partner is accepted from the contract, from the customer hierarchy, from both, or without a check
we use AA for additional authorized sold-to parties for release orders and AW for additional authorized ship-to parties
in the standard partner setup for release orders, KAB contains the AA and AW partner functions; we verify the assigned procedure in the target template
we can default contract dates and lifecycle controls through date determination and contract-profile settings instead of relying on manual entry

data_hinges.changes: the commercial ceiling and completion state for goods contracts
the remaining open entitlement
whether a release or coverage decision can still reference the agreement
which products are valid for release
customer-level material eligibility independently of contract consumption
whether a site may procure or sell a product in the Retail assortment model
whether the goods release is authorized
what commercial conditions are inherited or redetermined in the release order
which master terms apply in a master-contract hierarchy

data_hinges.data: service product / billing plan / SLA context
data_hinges.changes: service coverage and periodic or follow-on billing behavior
which additional sold-to parties are allowed to place release orders
which additional ship-to parties are offered for release-order delivery

data_hinges.data: contract start / end date and duration
data_hinges.changes: whether a release remains valid and when follow-up or cancellation logic becomes relevant
when direct contract billing is due and how remaining dates are adjusted after target-value changes

impact_summary: We keep the long-term commercial entitlement in the contract and create executable demand through release orders when delivery dates and quantities become concrete.
For quantity contracts, we control released quantity. For value contracts, we control released value and can also choose direct contract billing through a billing plan.
We keep automatic open-contract search separate from copy control: search helps us find the agreement, while copy control governs the contract-to-order reference and data transfer.

When we use a sales scheduling agreement instead, we keep the recurring operational quantities and dates in delivery schedules and schedule lines rather than creating a separate call-off order for every release.
We can bill a value contract in two different ways: we either bill each release-order flow, or we make the value contract itself billing relevant through a billing plan.
We keep release authorization separate from ordinary partner determination: AA controls additional releasing sold-to parties, while AW controls additional receiving ship-to parties.
We can use date determination and a contract profile to default lifecycle data such as date rules, cancellation handling, and follow-up actions where the target contract type supports it.
constraints: A quantity contract contains target quantity and commercial data but no schedule of concrete delivery dates and quantities.
A value contract is more flexible: the releasable product scope can be one material or a broader set such as a product hierarchy or assortment module, depending on product and deployment scope.
The classic assortment-module model for value contracts and the current product-hierarchy model are not identical deployment assumptions. Verify the target edition before configuring.
General SD Material Listing/Exclusion is customer-material eligibility based on condition technique. It does not consume a contract target.
Retail Assortment Management is a site/product listing model with listing periods. It is not the same object as a value-contract assortment module.
Master-contract availability and behavior are deployment-sensitive; check the target S/4HANA edition before designing around it.

Service contracts are a neighboring long-term agreement model. In current S/4HANA Service they integrate with service order management, billing, pricing and financials rather than following the normal goods release-order chain.
The release order must stay inside contract validity and product-scope rules; over-release behavior is a deliberate control decision.
When we use down-payment processing for a sales quantity contract, we design the billing plan, delivery block, incoming-payment release, and final clearing as one end-to-end control.
When we bill a value contract directly, we treat billing-plan corrections and target-value changes as part of the contract design rather than assuming normal release-order billing will solve them.
A value contract with a billing plan is not automatically billed while it has not been completely released.
If we reduce a value-contract target after billing-plan dates have already been billed, SAP does not automatically prove that we have not overbilled; we may need a credit memo for the difference.

Classic standard document examples such as OR for release orders, WA for direct value-contract billing, and KAB for release-order partner determination are useful memory anchors, but we verify document types and assignments in the target S/4HANA deployment before treating them as design facts.
Partner authorization for release orders is a header-level contract control; we do not design it as an item-by-item authorization model.
lead_questions: What are we asking the customer to commit to: quantity, spend, umbrella terms, service coverage, or a rolling delivery schedule?
Where do we keep the executable delivery dates and quantities?
Which order type may release against the contract, and what do we copy or redetermine?
Do we bill the release-order flow or the value contract itself?
If we bill the contract directly, what does the billing plan do when target value changes?
Who is allowed to release: only the contract sold-to, AA partners, hierarchy partners, or a combination?
Which AW ship-to parties may receive the released goods?
Do we use a contract profile and date rules to default validity, cancellation, or follow-up behavior?
What do we want to happen at 100% consumption, expiry, renewal, or over-release?
For a quantity contract, do we require a down payment before we allow delivery?
Are we solving a contract problem, or should we use a sales scheduling agreement because the customer already sends recurring quantities and dates?
